utterances.text: It is a fact, isn't it, that at the very beginning of the war and the conflict, some members of the paramilitaries killed a mentally disabled Croat, and it was then that Croatian forces blocked the Knezevo-Travnik road, or it was, in other words, Knezevo-Skender Vakuf road, and it continued to be blocked throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That man was mentally unstable. The victim, I mean. And the Croatian side didn't really block the road. That road passed along the Ugar River. It was a kind of natural border, a canyon, and that road was controlled from high up above the canyon from both sides. It was neither theirs or ours. It was not safe for passage any more for anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because this road was blocked. Actually, that was the reason why the old road passing by Koricanske Stijene was used; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While you were at the post of the chief of the public security station -- first of all, let me ask you this: When was it that you were appointed to that post, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime on the 6th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I suppose it's not controversial that the then minister, Alija Delimustafic, signed the decision on your appointment.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout 1992, while you were the chief of the public security station, you insisted that the police and the police officers should comply with the law in their work.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That pertains to the law of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Law on Internal Affairs, and also on the Law on Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska, which was, in essence, identical to the other one.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your statements, I found your claim that in 1992 a total number of homicides or murders in the territory covered by the public security station in Knezevo, the total number was seven, seven murders.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six in 1992 and one in late 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And as for the victims, five were Muslims, one was a Croat, and one victim was a Serb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The one Croat that we mentioned here was this unfortunate man that we mentioned a little while ago, this mentally ill person killed by the paramilitaries right at the beginning of the conflict; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, since you were the chief, each of these crimes, and I'm talking about murders, were dealt with in accordance with the law on the -- on internal affairs and in accordance with your powers, and a criminal complaint was filed to the appropriate public prosecutor's office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm mindful of the time. Perhaps now would be the appropriate time for a break. I think I have about 10 to 15 minutes at most in my cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, in all the cases that we mentioned, the seven murders that we've been talking about, and other serious crimes, if I understand you correctly, the police did its job in accordance with the laws in force at the time in terms of investigating those crimes.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the only exception is the murder of this Croat, ethnic Croat, because it was impossible to reach the crime scene safely and to perform all those tasks that we've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So after the murder of this ethnic Croat the police set off, but the road was already blocked and the police were unable to reach the scene and do the on-site investigation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me, with regard to the murders, were you able to identify the perpetrators in each and every case?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The perpetrators remained unidentified in all of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Just one last question. In the municipality of Knezevo, where the demarcation line was bordering with the area controlled by the enemy, a certain number of convoys actually passed through; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And your public security station, in line with the law after all, did not play any part in those movements or transfers of population, exchanges of population.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: One last question then. The exchange of population at the demarcation line was carried out under the control of the military unit, the one that we've been talking about, the one that held Knezevo as part of its area of responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I just have a few questions. I'll try to keep this as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, Mr. Krejic. Now, yesterday you were asked by Mr. Krgovic, this is at transcript page 14078, what Mr. Zupljanin had said at the first meeting held at CSB Banja Luka on the 23rd, 24th of August, and you'd mentioned that Mr. Drljaca had wanted to conceal the murder, and Mr. Zupljanin had said, "One murder cannot be concealed. These murders cannot be concealed." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, do you recall if Mr. Zupljanin mentioned any specific reason why these murders in particular could not be concealed?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief Zupljanin did not insist only on the fact that it was impossible to conceal the murders. He insisted that he refuse to conceal them, that he was absolutely opposed to any effort to conceal the murders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Krejic, are you aware if any survivors from the killings had crossed over into Muslim-held territory and spoken to the media there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the first meeting, Chief Zupljanin told us about that. He told us that he had received information to the effect that there were survivors who had crossed the demarcation line, which was right there in the canyon of the Ugar River, and that they made a statement of sorts for Radio Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on now. Earlier on today, you were shown a document. This is the document which the instructions on the use of the Territorial Defence. The number was 1D04-2409, and you were read -- or at least you agreed with the proposition that in the state of imminent threat of war the police forms a part of the Territorial Defence and carry out combat and other tasks. Now, does this mean that the Territorial Defence takes over command of the police or that they simply co-ordinate and work together?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to answer a question phrased like this. In early 1992, there was no state of war. It had not been declared. And as far as I know, there was no imminent threat of war as such, and the Territorial Defence or the armed forces which comprised the Territorial Defence as one of its components, in the depth of the territory where there was no fighting worked side by side with the police in the manner that you've described, co-ordination, making arrangements. And in the combat zone, especially when police units were engaged in fighting, they were strictly subordinated to the Territorial Defence of the Yugoslav People's Army, later on of the Republika Srpska Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: On that topic, Mr. Zecevic put to you that, as you've just said, in the performance of combat tasks, police come under the command of the military unit. An article or paragraph of these instructions was not cited. You have those instructions in front of you, and I'm just going to ask you if you're aware of any particular article in those instructions that states that's the case?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to repeat the last part of your question. I fear I haven't really understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic's proposition that when combat tasks are performed you come under -- police units would come under the control of the military, can you yourself cite an article in those instructions that states that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And which article would that be?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KREJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was at page 12 or 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: We'll move on from there. If we perhaps look at Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before you move away from this, I had myself a question relating to this issue of resubordination of police forces for the purpose of combat operations, because the way I understand, and I refer to you, Mr. Witness, to correct me if my understanding is wrong, but during the armed conflict, that is to say from April and onwards in 1992, the police would normally not be taking part in combat operations, but from time to time the local army command would request assistance of police forces to take part in a particular combat operation, and for those purposes the army would then assume command and control over those policemen who were resubordinated to the army for that particular purpose, and when that operation was completed, the policemen would be returned to their civil command. First of all, my first question: Is this correctly understood, or have I -- or did I get it wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, excellently put. Let me just add one minor detail. The Supreme Command could also call for the use of the police units, not just local commands, local military commands. The Supreme Command could also make such a demand. But as for the rest, you've really defined it perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And thank you for this addition, which makes sense. My next question would be: What then about the police brigade? Did the same situation apply to the police brigade, namely that -- that most of the time the police brigade would remain under civilian command and do the police work that was needed in the local area, and then from time to time the police brigade would be subordinated to the army for a particular purpose, or was the police brigade at all times put under the command and control of the armed forces? In other words, was there a difference between the -- the regular police force that was employed at the SJBs and under the CSB on the one hand and then the police brigade on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the police brigade, specifically the brigade that was deployed in Posavina, it was deployed there on the demand of the Supreme Command. So it's the same procedure but a higher level. The local military units demanded that the personnel from the local public security stations be engaged, and as for the brigade, a demand was made by the Supreme Command or a corps command from the Ministry of the Interior or security services centre. As regards the personnel in the brigade, those were police officers who performed their day-to-day police work and during lulls on the front line the brigade did not exist for all intents and purposes. And when the situation at the front became more difficult and when the Supreme Command made this request, then the ordinary police officers would form a police brigade and be dispatched to the front, resubordinated to the army. And we can see that the brigade commander in this particular case was, in fact, an active-duty serviceman in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And please forgive me for putting these questions. It's difficult for someone who is not a part of the events to fully understand what -- how this operated. But from what you have just said, I would conclude that -- that the police brigade was -- was a unit that was established on a regular basis so as to say -- so as to be able to participate in reinforcement of the combat operations carried out by the armed forces, but then as you said, when the situation at the front line lulled or when there was a pause in the fighting, then the police brigade sort of more or less fell apart and people will go back to their -- the police officers would go back to their normal police duties and yet again work under the command of their civilian police superiors. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excellent. Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I have no further questions now at this time either for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krejic, for your testimony before the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. Thank you, sir. The usher will escort you from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn -- yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I have one intervention in the transcript if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just bear with me, Your Honours, one second. It's page 4. It's line 7, 8, and 9. It was -- it was recorded like this -- that was my submission at the beginning of today's session, and it's recorded here as: "The Trial Chamber knows that the Defence is obliged to state its position on the motion pertaining to 92 bis witness. We will agree to that." That is not what I said. What I -- I'm pretty sure that's not what I said, because it's not in my -- in my notes, and -- and I don't know where it come from -- where it came from. What I wanted to -- to explain to Your Honours was that we have three cumulative things which are going on at the same time, that is, the 92 bis witnesses which we have to review in order to able to agree with the Prosecution about it. That was one thing. The other was exhumations, and the third thing is our day-to-day preparation of cross-examination. That is the only clarification I wanted to do in the transcript so that it might not be understood as our agreement. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Dobbyn, is your next witness here?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and if I may be excused Mr. Olmsted will be taking over this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, there was a point that you wanted to raise -- you wanted to reserve a half hour today --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe fifteen minutes will be enough for that matter now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So are you suggesting that we call the witness in and then take a 15 -- or how are you suggesting we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, we would like to start with the witness and see how far we can get and then leave 15 minutes at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to clarify, there has been some progress over the breaks in terms of the issues, the outstanding issues, and that is why we only request 15 minutes at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the reason we're going to proceed this way is this witness has been here since 3.00, and probably my error, but I did promise him that he would start today, so I think it will be good that we can at least get him sworn in and, of course, the bulk of our examination will be tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Why I was inquiring as to whether he was here is because, as a matter of courtesy to him, what I would have done was to invite him into the courtroom and explain the reason for the delay, but if you feel you can usefully use the time, then we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Why not. Let's at least get the provisional questions over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good evening, sir. I trust you can here me. Would you kindly make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may be seated. The solemn declaration that you have just taken obliges you to speak the truth under pain of the -- being -- having imposed upon you the penalties for perjury which this Tribunal is empowered to impose should you give false or misleading testimony. Could you begin by giving us your name, date of birth, and profession, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Marinko Kovacevic, born 29th of September, 1956. I have a law degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And is that your profession now or in the past, working as a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My current occupation is higher professional assistance for licensing affairs in an agency for insurance in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you testified previously either before this Tribunal or before any of the courts in one of the countries that would have comprised the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified before the BH state court in 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you have been called as a witness before this Tribunal by the Prosecution, and the procedure, as with most tribunals is that the side calling you would begin by asking you questions, and then the side opposite. In this case there are two accused persons, so counsel for each of those would have the right to cross-examine you, and then the Prosecution could ask you questions arising out of that, and at the conclusion of that, or indeed at any point before that, if the Chamber has any questions, it may ask you directly. Now, the Prosecution has indicated that they would spend three hours -- three hours with you, and the -- counsel for the first accused has indicated that he would need -- require two hours for his cross-examination, and counsel for the second accused, three hours. The -- I should explain to you that although you have been here, as we have been informed, since 3.00, the reason for the delay is that the nature of trials is that inevitably there are procedural and other issues that arise which inhibit the flow of the trial as smoothly as we all would have liked. So we trust that you were not unduly inconvenienced by having to wait longer than you expected. The ordinary sitting times of the court are with the afternoon sittings we begin at 2.15 and rise for the day at 7.00, and then morning sittings would begin at 7.00 -- sorry, at 9.00 and end at 1.45. In this case, your testimony begins in an evening sitting, so we would be rising in about a half hour, but indeed counsel for the Prosecution has indicated that there are certain procedural matters with which they wish to deal, so you would excused a little before the Chamber rises, and we will resume in this courtroom at 9.00 tomorrow morning and sit through, as I said, until 1.45. Now, within those beginning and ending times there are breaks for the technical reason that the tapes by which these proceedings are recorded have to be changed every 90 minutes, so the actual session does not last longer than 90 minutes. Indeed, it's more like an hour and 20 minutes, an hour and 25 minutes. And the -- those breaks are also used by counsel and the parties to -- for their own comfort. But if, of course, at any point before a regular break you need to take an adjournment, you would indicate that to us and we would accommodate you. The -- and with that, I would invite Mr. Olmsted to begin his cross -- his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to start out by just briefly going over your legal background. From 1984 to 1990, you were deputy public prosecutor in Banja Luka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then from 1990 until mid-1992, you worked for a private business.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And then -- and then in August of 1992, you were appointed once again to the position of deputy prosecutor in the Banja Luka basic prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Who was the basic prosecutor in Banja Luka at the time of your appointment?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nebojsa Pantic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how long did you remain as a deputy public prosecutor in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Until 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And at that time what position were you holding from that point forward?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In 1998, I was acting prosecutor until I was officially appointed as prosecutor on the 24th of December, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And how long were you basic prosecutor in Banja Luka for? Till what year?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Until March 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have on the screen Exhibit P264.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, what we're looking at are the minutes from the 19th session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in BiH held on the 12th of August, 1992, in Banja Luka. If I can draw your attention to item number 1, we see a number of persons who were appointed as Judges and Deputy Prosecutors in Banja Luka at this session, and I believe it also includes your name.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you confirm for us, were these, in fact, the prosecutors and judges who held these positions in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the judges and prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I just want you to focus on 1992. At any time in 1992, were there any additional judicial or prosecutorial appointments made?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: None that you're aware of then?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at Exhibit 2D71. What we have before us is the first page in the police file for a case involving the murder of eight unidentified persons by an unknown perpetrator. Mr. Kovacevic, are you familiar with this case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you became familiar with it in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Following the regular procedure, the basic public prosecutor, the chief, Mr. Nebojsa Pantic, entrusted this case to me as deputy prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So just to be clear, Mr. Panic -- or Pantic came to you and assigned you as prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Pantic. Yes, he did. He gave me this criminal complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could take a look at page 2 of the B/C/S and page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is the on-site investigation report by the investigative judge, dated 8 August, 1992, and we see that the basic prosecutor Pantic participated in this on-site investigation. Did you receive a copy of this report?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Under the procedures that existed back in 1992, would the prosecutor's office have received this report from the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can just turn to the next page on both B/C/S and English, and we'll just show you one of these. But there are eight of them. These are records of forensic examination by Dr. Dragutin Savjak, also dated 8 August, 1992, and did you receive these reports as well?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And these minutes, these records, were part of the case file, of the prosecutor's case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And they would come along with the on-site investigation report?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When the expertise is finished, it is submitted usually with the on-site investigation report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to return to page 1 in both the B/C/S and the English. And what we're looking at is the unknown perpetrator criminal report from CSB Banja Luka, dated the 26th of August, 1992. And just to confirm, is this the criminal report that you received for this case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall on what date this criminal report was received by the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was received in the beginning of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 2957. What we have in front of us is the KTN log-book for the basic prosecutor's office in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 26. And if we can look along the right-hand side page and zoom in on entry 2284.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, can you confirm that entry 2284 pertains to this case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, column two contains the date that the report was received on, and for this particular entry we have just a checkmark, but if we can scroll up a little bit to about three entries above it, we see the date 7 September 1992, and directly below this entry 2284, there's the date 10 September 1992. Based on this can we conclude that the report, the criminal report, was received between the 7th and the 10th of September?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And since we're on this entry, if we look over in column 16 and 17, we see a date of 26 May 2000. Can you tell us what occurred in the year 2000 with regard to this case file?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, there was a change in jurisdiction so that this -- these cases were given to the competent district prosecutor's office in Banja Luka, and the district prosecutor's office in Banja Luka, according to this record, received this on the 26th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And as of the date of the transfer, was this case still classified as an unknown perpetrator criminal case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's a KTN case, meaning that an unknown perpetrator is involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you know -- we see that this criminal report arrived at the prosecutor's office sometime between the 7th and the 10th of September, but that the crime occurred towards the beginning of August. Do you know why it took a month for the police to submit this report to your office?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why, why it took that long.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's a good point to stop, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, we, as I indicated, are taking the adjournment for the day. You having been sworn as a witness, you cannot have any communication with counsel from either side, and in such conversations as you may have with persons outside of the courtroom, you cannot discuss your testimony. So the usher would now escort you from the courtroom, and we will resume your testimony at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, my learned friends from the Defence raised four issues at the commencement of the proceedings today, and I propose to deal with each of them in turn. Coming from the southern hemisphere, I am going to do them in the opposite direction from which they were raised, simply because the last two matters can be dealt with fairly briefly and the first two matters require a little bit more explanation. Now, we have had some discussions over the breaks, and that is why -- and we think we've received -- or reached a compromise situation on the substantive issues, which is why we think we only need this abbreviated time at this juncture. So firstly it's the -- if I can firstly address the issue of the Mladic material, which was one of the last matters raised by my learned friend. Just to clarify a couple of issues. Firstly, the audio recordings and the videos from the Mladic material has been disclosed to the Defence. It was disclosed on the 23rd of July of this year. There was a reference to a -- a MUP report from my learned friend. Now, a Ministry of the Interior report was disclosed to the Defence earlier this week, simply relates -- in redacted form, it simply relates to the search and seizure of the material and has nothing to do with any of the issues relevant to this case in 1992. I'm not aware of any additional Ministry of the Interior report that my learned friend referred to, and if he could enlighten me I would appreciate that, but we're not aware of any other Ministry of the Interior reports related to the Mladic material. The issue was raised by my learned friend in respect of the testimony of the military expert that we propose to call, Ewan Brown. Now, he is not scheduled to testify imminently and for this very reason we have deferred his testimony in light of the new a Mladic material and to ensure that the Defence have enough time to review it. We have not commissioned a new report from him, but he is currently reviewing the material, and if there are any matters which need expansion from his report, when he comes back to us on that we will be seeking leave to do that orally, formally at that juncture, but that's a premature submission from my friend in that regard. The second issue I want to deal with is the general issue of disclosure overload and the amount of work that everybody is doing at this -- at this current time. The -- we are at a position where we are indeed disclosing a lot of material to the Defence. That is because we are disclosing the material for the new witnesses. We're under very, very strict time frames to do that, because we need to call these witnesses six weeks from the moment of disclosure in accordance with your ruling. Now, it's the beginning of September, and we will end our current witness list, on my schedule anyway, in the first week in October. So we need to have disclosed everything for these new witnesses six weeks prior to that date. So we are working very hard to get all the -- all of that out, and that is what -- it is coming to the Defence thick and fast at the moment. Now, amongst that material is some new material that may or may not relate to the -- the witnesses on the current list, but that is -- that is the bulk of the material that is going to the Defence at this point. We are burdened with this obligation under 66(B), triggered by the Defence, to disclose everything to them, not just Rule 68 material but everything that may be relevant to the issues in this case and that was their choices to trigger that 66(B) rule. We're complying with that and we're doing so fairly liberally to ensure or to try and ensure that we catch everything. So that's the -- that's where both teams are at, at the moment in terms of disclosure. The major issue that I need to address, or the more important one at this juncture anyway, is the testimony of Witness ST-197 next week. The -- and there are two aspects of that: One is the amendment to the 65 ter summary, and the other is the disclosure of the documents. Firstly, in relation to the 65 ter summary, this is not an amendment, as my learned friend put it, to the 65 ter list. Now, yesterday he listed a number of issues and a number of times spoke about how many times the Prosecution had sought to amend the 65 ter list and so forth. This is not a situation like this. We are seeking to amend the 65 ter summary for this witness. We are obliged to file that summary in June last year. The witness was seen in March and then in August again this year. There are three issues which Your Honour, Judge Delvoie, highlighted earlier today. My colleague Mr. Dobbyn addressed one of those. The remaining two are -- well, firstly the meeting with Stojan Zupljanin and the Kotor Varos issues. I'll put them together because they're inter-related. That issue was contained in his statement in March 2010 and was disclosed to the Defence on the 15th of April. So the Defence have known about that issue since that time. The videos or the Kotor Varos videos which are a part of the documents which are the second part, but they were found after that date, and Your Honours may, if you wanted to track the -- how -- how we came to about those videos, it's all contained in the statement of our investigator Michael Koehler, which is attached our recent motion to add those videos to our 65 ter list. So the Defence have known about that meeting and the Kotor Varos issues since April 2010. The last issue is that of resubordination. Now, Your Honours are aware that's a live issue in this case, and this witness is one of the few military witnesses that you -- you will hear from. He was -- this issue was raised and discussed with him at the second interview we did with him in early August during the recess, and it was at that time that we canvassed the issues with him and this was disclosed to the Defence on the 10th of August. So they've known about that since that time. Now, my understanding from the Defence is that they will agree that it's appropriate for the Prosecution to lead evidence on those three new issues and expand the 65 ter summary, and they wouldn't be opposing it if they had more time to review the documents which were disclosed yesterday, and I'm just going to dovetail into that now because I think although we have reached a proposal which we want to jointly put to you about his testimony, I just want to clarify for the record the documents which were disclosed yesterday. Now, my learned friend said there were 687 pages of material which -- at least of which 50 per cent were relevant which needed to be reviewed meticulously by them. There were, in fact, nine documents, separate documents which were disclosed yesterday. The first three were transcripts from the new videos. Now, the videos themselves were disclosed to them in early August. We formally sought to add them in a motion filed last week, and in the intervening time, and we have sent them to our services for transcription, and so in my submission this is not new evidence that is available to the Defence. It's simply a different form of the evidence that they previously had. The fourth one is the transcription of the video from Kotor Varos which Your Honours have already ruled into evidence and admitted to our 65 ter list. It's 65 ter 3623. It's the transcript of that video. Now, Your Honours, these transcripts are very difficult to do, because they -- the quality is very bad, and so we've had to spend some time trying to get the transcriptions right in order to provide them to the Court and the interpreters when we propose to actually formally tender them. So that's the first four documents out of the nine. The fifth document or series of documents was 50 photos, and one of them contains a photo of one of the accused. The rest do not, but they are a series, and that's what -- that's what are contained in that -- that range of documents. The sixth document has just been used by the Defence today and added by Your Honours to the law library. So that is a document of over 200 pages long, and forms part of the 687 that they were complaining about, but has, in fact, been tendered by them today and alternatively we agreed to just add it to the law library. The next document is a similar document. It's an instruction on civil affairs. It's a regulation. It's 11 pages. So it falls into the same category as the previous one. The last two documents are new. One is a handwritten diary from the president of the municipal Executive Board. It's one page. And the last document is -- is a chart which -- of the military structure drawn by the witness. So that's, in summary, the documents that were sent to them yesterday. In my submission, they're -- their application to adjourn the entire testimony of the witness on the grounds that they have to review 687 pages of material is misleading. In fact, when, you break it down there's two pages of new documents, one new photo, and the rest of the material has been explained. Despite that, Your Honours, we have had discussions over the break, and in light of the fact that the current witness has only just started and will go into tomorrow, possibly over 'till Monday, it's been agreed with the Defence that we will call ST-197 directly after he finishes, the current witness finishes next week, and then we will defer his cross-examination. That solves two problems. One, it means that he won't be held over the four-week long -- the four-day, sorry, weekend, and it means the Defence have agreed that the Prosecution will be able to lead new evidence -- well, the expanded evidence under the new 65 ter summary. So the joint proposal, Your Honours, is that we continue as scheduled and call Witness ST-197 next week, that we defer his cross-examination, and it will be for a date to be advised because I'd like to be able to speak with the witness himself and organise that around his schedule, and bring him back possibly in about three or four weeks to commence and conclude his cross-examination. And on that basis, the Defence have agreed that the -- the Prosecution can lead the evidence on the expanded topics which are relevant to the issues in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pidwell. Do either Defence counsel have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honours, a verification. I'm not going to touch this because we agreed, and we hereby withdraw our -- our opposition to the amendment of 65 ter summary. That is -- that is correct. I was referring to the summary. I -- I mistakenly referred to the list. Your Honours, the point is not whether the statement or the video or the documents are disclosed at a certain point in time. It is -- what is important for us is that we have to know if this area will be explored by the Prosecution. So if the 65 ter summary stays the same, so they are not calling him for these particular issues that he mentions in his testimony and we can disregard them, or maybe we can use it, but the point of the matter is late notice in the change of the 65 ter summary, that they indeed want to -- to explore that -- that area with this witness. That is the point of the problem. But I'm not going again into this. The second thing, Your Honours, what I was referring to Mladic, I have seen what -- what so far we have been disclosed with is the diaries and the 20 or 30 hours of audio and video material. However, I know that in case Perisic and in Gotovina and in some other cases, another 150 hours of audio and video material additionally has been -- has been disclosed, and I saw the -- the actual Ministry of Interior report confirming the contents of that material. So that's an expertise of MUP of Republika Srpska on that particular material, and it has couple of hundred of pages. And if my learned friends can knock on the door on their friends in the office, they will probably be able to find that out. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have anything, except that we agree with the Prosecution how to sort out the problem with Witness ST-197.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We will formally rule on the joint proposal at the start of tomorrow's sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I have one question, Ms. Pidwell. Do you have another witness available to fill the gap that eventually will occur?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: In short, no, Your Honour. Ms. Korner is going to ask for five hours in total in chief with Witness ST-197 in light of the video material and expanded topics. We -- and so we envisage there will be a -- despite that application, there will be a gap, because we don't have a back-up witness to fill the gap for next week at this late juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. We take the adjournment until 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
